messages.subject: problems with implementing custom functions
parts:
Dear colleagues!

I am trying to implement several custom distributions, such as one of the skewed t distributions.
I am totally new to stan, so I started with an attempt to implement a very simple model for fitting parameters of the exponentially distributed data. However, I quickly got stuck because three different methods I played with return inconsistent results, and I really want to know why, and what am I doing wrong. Details below.

I used three different ways, all of them were mentioned in the stan reference manual (2.6.2) - two functions (chapter 42.5. Exponential Distribution) and one method which is based on the log probability (chapter 16. Custom Probability Functions).

In sum, my model looks like:

model < - 
“data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
}
parameters {
  real lambda1;
  real lambda2;
  real lambda3;
}
model {
  y ~ exponential(lambda1);
  increment_log_prob(exponential_log(y, lambda2));
  increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[N]*lambda3);
}”

Sample from the exponential distribution and code for fitting lambdas (all in R):

y <- rexp(10000, 1.648721)
mcmc_samples <- stan(model_code = model,
                  data = list(N = length(y), y = y),
                  chains=9, iter=30000, warmup=20000,
                  verbose = F, refresh = -1)

I did not set the bounds for lambdas, in result stan() function returned a lot of warnings. One of them:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::exponential_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Inverse scale parameter is -1.8615:0, but must be > 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine, but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.


Of course these steps are common but the results are extremely confusing. Simple built-in functions fitted the parameter of the exponentially distributed data amazingly close to the origin parameter. However, the parameter fitted by the third method fell way far from the original value:

> mcmc_samples
Inference for Stan model: model_simple.

post-warmup draws per chain=10000, total post-warmup draws=90000.

and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at

What am I doing wrong? Why do the methods return such different results?
And how do I implement a custom function correctly?

Thanks a lot,
Philipp

The first thing you should do is to declare your parameters with constraints. Instead of lambda1, lambda2, and lambda3 being declared as real, they should really be declared as real<lower=0>.

This one is simple. You need a for loop. The current code:
increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[N]*lambda3);

is only incrementing the log probability by the likelihood of the Nth element of the data.

It should look like:
    for (n in 1:N)
      increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[n]*lambda3);

If you wanted to be more efficient, you'd simplify the algebra and take the log only once, maybe sum the data in transformed data and multiply once too.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problems with implementing custom functions
parts:
Right. To follow up on what Daniel said, you want to replace
this:
> increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[N]*lambda3);

with

increment_log_prob(N * log(lambda3) - sum(y * lambda));

with y declared as

vector<lower=0>[N] y;

Declaring as vector lets you do vector arithmetic, like multiplying
by a scalar. Putting the bounds in does error checking on the data
when it's read, which is not required, but is helpful for catching errors.

It's critical that you have the constraints in the parameters
as Daniel stated --- Stan will not sample efficiently (including
perhaps not at all) when you have parameters that have values that
match their declared constraint but have 0 density in the model.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problems with implementing custom functions
parts:
Our built-in sampling statements do all this for you.


> On Jul 5, 2015, at 7:54 AM, Philipp Upravitelev <uprav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

> Unfortunately I can't understand the logic of vector arithmetics. Well, I can understand it in simple cases like an exponential function (pdf, of course).

> But it is difficult to me to write this (lognormal pdf):

> for (n in 1:N)
> increment_log_prob(-log(y[n] * sigma * ml) - pow((log(y[n]) - mu), 2)/(2 * pow(sigma, 2)));
>
> in vectorized form. Could you help me with it? Where I should use "sum" and multiplication by N, and why?

What exactly are you trying to do? If you have a lognormal PDF, you can
just write

y ~ lognormal(mu, sigma);

And the sampling statement will drop any constant terms not needed to
define the density up to a proportion.

I don't know what the term ml is.

You just want to do the algebra. You have a sum of N terms.
Some of them will be repeated, so you can pull them out of the
lop and multiply by N, for instance a -log(sigma) term.

- Bob
